chunks.disease_title: Chế độ ăn cho người Tiểu đường (Diabetes)
chunks.source: Diet for Diabetic Patients_ Recommended Foods, Foods to Avoid, and Dietary Targets.pdf
chunks.section: Background
chunks.text: Diet is a main part of diabetes treatment for all people with diabetes. The best diet is not one rigid plan, but an individualized, balanced eating pattern that supports blood sugar, weight, blood pressure, and blood fats. Diet therapy is a basic part of care in diabetes, no matter the type, and it works best when it is built as a balanced eating pattern rather than a special or extreme "diabetic diet." In practice, meal plans are usually individualized to the person's body size, target weight, energy use, physical activity, culture, ethnicity, eating habits, insulin regimen, and any other health problems. This is because the main goals of dietary treatment are broad: keep blood glucose near target, support healthy body weight, and help control blood pressure and blood lipids while still providing enough calories and overall nutritional balance. Across sources, some general themes stay consistent even when exact macronutrient ratios differ: avoid refined sugar and limit saturated fat, choose healthier fats and fiber-rich foods, and plan meals in a structured way that fits the person's daily life.

chunks.section: Foods and dietary components to limit or avoid
chunks.text: People with diabetes are usually advised to limit foods that raise blood sugar quickly and foods that add excess calories, saturated fat, salt, or sugar. In practice, this means cutting back on sugary drinks, sweets, refined grains and starches, and heavily processed high-fat foods. Avoid sugary drinks and other fast-absorbing sugars. Sweetened drinks, sweets, chocolate, and other isolated sources of rapidly absorbed sugar can raise blood glucose quickly and are commonly advised against except for treating hypoglycemia. Limit refined starches and low-fiber grain foods. White bread, pastries, refined flour products, and other fiber-poor starches are commonly discouraged, while wholemeal or whole-grain versions are preferred. Be careful with high-glycemic-index carbohydrate foods. Foods with a high glycemic index can raise blood glucose rapidly, so carbohydrate choices are often guided by GI and portion control. Do not let staple starch portions get too large. Some guidance specifically says staple foods should not be excessive and total daily calories should be controlled. Keep added sugar low. A "light" diet pattern with less sugar is repeatedly recommended for diabetes care. Limit high-fat foods, especially less healthy fats. Guidance commonly recommends a lower-fat eating pattern overall, which fits with earlier advice in this summary to favor unsaturated fats over heavier, more energy-dense fat sources. Limit salt. chunks.section: Background: diet as a cornerstone of fatty liver disease management
chunks.text: Diet is a main part of treating fatty liver disease because it can help reduce body weight, improve insulin sensitivity, and improve liver-related markers. The strongest overall message from these studies is that sustained calorie reduction and a healthy dietary pattern, especially a Mediterranean-style pattern, matter more than any single "superfood." Diet is a core part of fatty liver disease care, not just a side recommendation. Reviews of NAFLD management note that dietary interventions play a crucial role, especially diets that support weight loss and better insulin sensitivity, and a meta-analysis found a dose-response link between greater calorie restriction and better weight loss and liver outcomes, supporting calorie reduction as a key part of management. More broadly, plant-based, high-fiber, low-fat eating has long been recommended in fatty liver disease. Other healthy dietary patterns may also help; for example, a randomized trial found that a Paleolithic diet reduced liver fat and improved insulin sensitivity- related measures in people with type 2 diabetes. chunks.section: Recommended dietary pattern for fatty liver disease
chunks.text: The most consistently recommended eating pattern for fatty liver disease is a calorie-controlled Mediterranean-style diet. In practice, that means mostly plant foods and minimally processed foods, with healthy fats like olive oil and nuts, regular fish, and much less sugar, refined carbs, and saturated fat. Across the papers provided, the clearest dietary recommendation is a Mediterranean-style pattern, and several reviews note that it is the diet most often recommended by clinical guidelines for NAFLD management. This pattern overlaps with what some authors call a "high-quality healthy diet": high in vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, nuts, seeds, and fiber; built around olive oil and other sources of monounsaturated and omega-3 fats; and lower in red meat, processed meat, sweets, refined carbohydrates, and highly processed foods. A practical way to think about the recommended pattern is: make most meals plant-forward, use olive oil instead of butter or other saturated fats, choose fish or poultry more often than red or processed meat, and keep added sugars and refined starches low. This matches the recurring findings that many patients with fatty liver disease tend to overconsume simple carbohydrates and saturated fat while under-consuming fiber and omega-3-rich foods, and that shifting in the opposite direction is helpful. Some reviews also describe plant-based patterns such as DASH-like or Mediterranean-related diets as useful because they lower saturated fat, red and processed meat, and refined carbohydrate intake while increasing antioxidant- and fiber-rich foods. chunks.section: Caloric restriction, macronutrient targets, and practical implementation
chunks.text: For most patients with fatty liver disease, the practical goal is a moderate calorie deficit that leads to slow, steady weight loss, not a crash diet. A useful template is a Mediterranean-style diet with controlled portions, moderate carbs, enough protein, and lower saturated fat. In practical terms, the diet usually works best when calories are reduced enough to produce gradual weight loss. The papers provided repeatedly recommend a deficit of about 500 to 1000 kcal/day, which usually aims for roughly 0.5 to 1.0 kg weight loss per week. Some papers also frame this as reducing usual intake by about 600 to 800 kcal/day or targeting about 25 to 30 kcal/kg/day of ideal body weight. In guideline-style summaries, example hypocaloric intake ranges are about 1000 to 1200 kcal/day for women and 1200 to 1500 kcal/day for men, though individual needs still depend on body size, age, activity, and medical context. For macronutrients, the broad message is to control total calories first, then shape those calories toward better quality. The cited papers suggest keeping carbohydrates around 40% to 45% of calories, with some reviews recommending less than 50%, while avoiding excess fructose and refined carbohydrate. Protein intake is often suggested at about 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day, which can help preserve lean mass during weight loss. Fat intake is generally shifted away from saturated fat and toward unsaturated fat: one review summarizes targets of <30% of calories from fat and <10% from saturated fat, while another emphasizes lowering cholesterol, saturated fat, and fructose and increasing n-3 polyunsaturated fats. Diet quality still matters even when weight loss is the main goal. Evidence summarized in these papers suggests that diets lower in fat, saturated fat, and glycemic load can improve liver fat and insulin sensitivity, even without major weight change, while overfeeding saturated fat appears to drive more liver fat accumulation than polyunsaturated fat. So the practical implementation is not just "eat less," but "eat less of the foods that worsen liver fat, and more of the foods that improve overall diet quality." A simple way to apply this day to day is to set up meals with portion control, keep sugary drinks and sweets out of the routine, and use a repeatable meal pattern rather than trying to count every nutrient perfectly. Patients can start by shrinking portions of calorie-dense foods, using vegetables and legumes to add fullness, choosing whole-grain or other high-fiber carbs in modest portions, and including a protein source at meals. This approach fits the calorie-deficit targets above while staying close to the Mediterranean-style pattern recommended across the papers. If patients want a simple bottom line: aim for steady weight loss, not rapid loss; use a moderate calorie deficit; keep carbs moderate and mostly high-fiber; get adequate protein; and keep saturated fat, fructose, and excess calories low. That is the most practical diet framework supported by the references provided.

chunks.disease_title: Chế độ ăn cho người Gút (Gout)
chunks.source: Diet for Gout Patients_ Recommended Foods, Dietary Patterns, and Foods to Avoid.pdf
chunks.section: Background: diet goals in gout management
chunks.text: The main diet goal in gout is to lower uric acid and reduce gout flares. Diet helps, but it works best along with weight control, good hydration, and medicines when needed. Gout happens when uric acid builds up and forms crystals in joints, so diet aims to reduce the body's uric acid load and lower the chance of crystal formation and flares. In practice, this means choosing an eating pattern that limits high-purine foods, avoids excess alcohol and sugar-sweetened drinks, supports a healthy body weight, and is easy to keep up over time rather than using short-term restrictive diets. Weight loss can help lower uric acid in people who are overweight, but crash dieting or fasting can make gout worse because rapid breakdown of body tissue can raise uric acid. Diet alone usually lowers uric acid only modestly, so many patients still need urate-lowering medicine; the goal is to use diet as one part of long-term gout control, not as the only treatment.

chunks.disease_title: Chế độ ăn cho người Gút (Gout)

chunks.section: Recommended dietary patterns and foods to encourage
chunks.text: For most gout patients, the best diet is not an extreme "gout diet," but a healthy pattern like DASH or Mediterranean-style eating. In practice, that means mostly plant foods, low-fat dairy, healthier protein choices, enough water, and a few foods such as cherries that may help lower flare risk. Rather than focusing only on single foods, many papers support using an overall healthy eating pattern such as the DASH diet or a Mediterranean-style diet, both of which emphasize fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while lowering saturated fat, added sugar, and red/processed meat intake. These patterns have been linked with lower serum urate and lower gout risk, and are often suggested for patients with mild gout or hyperuricemia, especially when gout overlaps with obesity, hypertension, or other metabolic problems. Foods to actively include are low-fat or nonfat dairy products such as skim milk and low-fat yogurt, which are repeatedly associated with lower uric acid or lower gout risk. Several reviews and guidelines also support getting protein more often from plant sources, including beans, lentils, legumes, and soy, instead of relying mainly on meat and seafood. (Hui et al., 2017) Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, nuts, and fiber-rich foods fit well in a gout-friendly diet. Importantly, plant foods that contain purines do not seem to raise gout risk the way animal purines do, so most patients do not need to avoid purine-rich vegetables; encouraging vegetable intake is supported by several sources. chunks.section: Foods and beverages to limit or avoid
chunks.text: The main things to cut back are alcohol, sugar-sweetened or high-fructose drinks, and high-purine animal foods. The clearest food triggers are beer and other alcohol, organ meats, red meat, shellfish, and some seafood such as sardines and anchovies. Alcohol: limit strongly, and avoid if it often triggers flares. Alcohol is one of the most consistent diet risks in gout guidance and studies, and risk rises even with short-term intake before an attack. Beer is often singled out, but wine and liquor can also increase flare risk, so patients should not assume wine is "safe." Beer and spirits deserve extra caution. Several reviews and guidelines highlight beer in particular, and some also point to spirits as a common problem. Older advice sometimes preferred wine over beer, but stronger prospective evidence shows that all major alcohol types can raise attack risk. Avoid sugar-sweetened drinks and foods rich in fructose or high-fructose corn syrup. This includes regular soda and other sweet drinks, and many guidelines also warn about fruit juice and sweetened soft drinks. These drinks are repeatedly linked with higher uric acid or higher gout risk. Regular soda is a notable item to avoid. Prospective cohort data found higher gout risk with increasing intake of sugar-sweetened soda, and some studies also found higher risk with orange juice or fruit juice, even though whole fruit does not show the same signal. chunks.section: Lifestyle and implementation considerations
chunks.text: Diet changes for gout work best when they are practical and long term, not extreme or short lived. The most useful habits are steady weight loss if overweight, good hydration, limiting alcohol and fructose, and using diet together with urate- lowering treatment when needed. Lifestyle advice is recommended for essentially all patients with gout, but the key is to make it sustainable in day-to-day life rather than trying to follow an overly strict "gout diet" for a short time. Reviews and guidelines consistently support focusing on a few high-yield changes: limit alcohol, avoid sugar-sweetened and other high-fructose drinks, reduce high-purine animal foods, avoid heavy meals, and work toward a healthier body weight if overweight. (Saliba et al., 2024) Weight management is an important part of implementation. For patients with overweight or obesity, gradual weight loss is commonly recommended because it can help both gout and related conditions such as hypertension, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome. At the same time, the overall message from recent reviews is not to rely on diet alone when gout is established; for many patients it is better to combine healthy eating with urate-lowering therapy instead of expecting strict food avoidance by itself to fully control disease. Hydration is also a practical part of care. Several sources advise adequate fluid intake, and older diet protocols often recommended roughly 2.5 to 3.5 liters per day, though the right amount should still fit the person's heart, kidney, and overall health status. chunks.section: Background: diet as first-line management for high cholesterol
chunks.text: Diet and other lifestyle changes are a standard first step for managing high cholesterol. The focus has shifted from just "low fat" to an individualized, whole-food eating pattern that helps improve blood lipids, weight, and overall heart risk. Diet is widely recommended as part of first-line treatment for high cholesterol, along with weight management and physical activity. Earlier cholesterol guidance emphasized a low-fat, low-cholesterol diet as part of therapeutic lifestyle changes, while newer nutrition guidance puts more weight on individualized eating patterns built around nutrient-rich, minimally processed whole foods in sensible portions. This shift matters because cholesterol management is not only about one nutrient; it is about a sustainable way of eating that improves blood lipids and overall cardiovascular risk over time. In practice, commonly recommended patterns include the Mediterranean diet and the DASH diet, both of which fit this whole-food approach and can support healthier cholesterol levels. (Evert et al., 2013)

chunks.section: Recommended dietary patterns and nutrient targets for high cholesterol
chunks.text: The best-supported eating patterns for high cholesterol are Mediterranean-style, DASH-style, vegetarian, and Portfolio-style diets built around whole plant foods, fish, and healthy fats. Most guidance agrees on cutting saturated fat, avoiding trans fat, keeping dietary cholesterol low, and adding soluble fiber and plant sterols. Rather than focusing on a single "cholesterol diet," most guidance supports a few similar eating patterns that lower LDL and improve overall heart risk: Mediterranean-style diets, DASH-style diets, vegetarian patterns, and the more targeted Portfolio diet. Mediterranean and vegetarian patterns can improve lipid profiles, and high-glycemic diets tend to worsen them. A Mediterranean diet is widely recommended for people with dyslipidemia and ASCVD prevention, with high use of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, and olive oil, moderate fish or seafood, and lower intake of red and processed meats. DASH-style eating can also fit LDL-lowering advice when it emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy, legumes, poultry, fish, nuts, and limited sweets and red meat. The Portfolio diet goes a step further by combining cholesterol- lowering foods such as nuts, plant proteins, viscous fiber, and plant sterols on top of a low-saturated-fat base, and it has shown clinically meaningful LDL reduction in hyperlipidemia. Across these patterns, the nutrient targets are fairly consistent. A common goal is to keep saturated fat below 10% of calories, and below 7% if LDL is high or hypercholesterolemia is present; trans fat should be avoided. Several guidelines also limit dietary cholesterol to less than 300 mg/day, with a stricter target of less than 200 mg/day often used when cholesterol remains elevated. Replacing

chunks.section: Foods and nutrients to emphasize
chunks.text: Build meals around plants: vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, nuts, and seeds. Use unsaturated fats like olive or canola oil, choose plant proteins often, and include fish regularly; add soluble fiber and plant sterols if you need more LDL lowering. The foods most worth emphasizing are the ones that reliably improve LDL and overall heart risk when they replace foods high in saturated fat. Across guidelines, this means eating plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and seeds, with fish and other lean proteins used regularly. Low-fat dairy can fit, and many recommendations also support fermented dairy such as yogurt and cheese, while still favoring lower saturated-fat choices overall. A practical way to do this is to make whole grains and other high-fiber plant foods the base of the diet. Whole grains, multigrain foods, beans, vegetables, and fruit help raise total fiber intake, and fiber has a cholesterol- lowering effect. Several sources also specifically encourage fish, including oily or "blue-back" fish, a few times per week. Among fats, the key point is not to fear all fat, but to use the right kinds. Olive, canola, peanut, and other vegetable oils rich in monounsaturated or polyunsaturated fat are preferred in place of butter, cream, or animal fat. Nuts and seeds are also useful because they provide unsaturated fats and can replace less healthy snacks or meats. Protein choices matter too. Plant proteins such as soy foods, beans, lentils, and nuts are repeatedly recommended, with fish next and poultry after that. chunks.section: Foods and dietary practices to limit or avoid
chunks.text: The main foods to cut back on are saturated fat, trans fat, refined carbs, sugary drinks, and ultra-processed foods. In day-to- day terms, that usually means less butter, cream, fatty and processed meats, fried foods, pastries, chips, and sugary drinks, and more attention to portion size and overall calorie intake. Avoid trans fats as much as possible. These are among the clearest "avoid" items in cholesterol advice. Common sources include partially hydrogenated oils, some margarines and shortenings, commercial baked goods, and foods made with oils repeatedly heated at high temperature. Limit saturated fat. The main foods to reduce are butter, cream, lard, ghee, palm oil, coconut oil, full-fat dairy, poultry skin, and fatty cuts of meat. Fried foods and foods cooked in butter or animal fat also fit here. Cut down on red meat, especially processed meat. Bacon, sausage, processed luncheon meats, and fatty or untrimmed red meat are commonly discouraged because they often bring both saturated fat and excess calories. Limit foods high in cholesterol if your LDL is high or your cardiovascular risk is high. Practical examples include egg yolks, organ meats such as liver and kidney, and some shellfish or shrimp. Several sources use a daily cholesterol limit of less than 300 mg, with less than 200 mg/day used in stricter therapeutic plans. Minimize refined starches, added sugars, and sugary drinks. This includes sweets, pastries, white-flour snack foods, sugar-sweetened beverages, and similar fast-digesting carbs. These foods can worsen triglycerides and make an otherwise "low-fat" diet less helpful. Avoid or sharply limit ultra-processed foods. This includes many packaged

chunks.section: Practical implementation and special considerations
chunks.text: The most useful way to follow a cholesterol-lowering diet is to make it practical: use regular meal routines, smaller portions, healthy cooking oils, and simple swaps from high-saturated-fat foods to plant foods, fish, and lean proteins. If cholesterol stays high, ask for formal diet counseling, and note that children, people with high triglycerides, and people with kidney or other medical conditions may need a more tailored plan. In practice, a cholesterol-lowering diet works best when it is turned into a repeatable routine rather than a short-term "diet." Several sources recommend regular eating schedules, portion control, and calorie intake matched to weight goals, since overeating can work against lipid improvement even if food choices are otherwise good. A simple rule is to eat until comfortably satisfied rather than full, keep portions moderate, and use a diet plan that fits the person's usual habits, preferences, weight, lipid pattern, and blood sugar status. For day-to-day cooking, use food preparation methods that lower saturated fat intake without making the diet hard to follow. Practical examples include cooking with olive, canola, or peanut oil instead of butter or animal fat, choosing lean protein sources, using more cereals, pulses, vegetables, fruit, and milk or dairy in balanced combinations, and avoiding reuse or repeated reheating of oil. Some guidance also suggests rotating vegetable oils to improve overall fatty acid balance. It also helps to think in terms of substitutions. Replace red and processed meat with fish, poultry, beans, lentils, soy foods, or other lean proteins; replace full-fat dairy with low-fat or nonfat versions; and replace foods rich

If extra LDL lowering is needed, daily soluble fiber and plant sterols can be added on top of these basic swaps. Lifestyle around the diet matters too. chunks.disease_title: Chế độ ăn cho người Bệnh thận (Kidney Disease)
chunks.source: Kidney Disease Diet Recommendations, Food Choices, and Foods to Avoid.pdf
chunks.section: Background: CKD diets are individualized by stage and complications
chunks.text: There is no single "kidney diet" that fits everyone with chronic kidney disease. Diet advice changes with CKD stage, lab results, symptoms, and problems like high potassium, high phosphorus, swelling, or poor nutrition. In CKD, food choices can help slow problems and reduce the buildup of substances that damaged kidneys cannot clear well, but the right diet depends on how advanced the disease is and what complications are present. As kidney function falls, patients often need to be more careful with protein, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and sometimes fluid intake, especially in later stages or when blood tests show hyperkalemia or hyperphosphatemia. For this reason, experts recommend a personalized diet rather than one fixed eating plan for all patients with CKD. Diet plans should be tailored to disease stage, metabolic stability, comorbidities, nutritional status, and the patient's food preferences and cultural background. This is also why some patients need protein restriction, while others, such as children with CKD or undernourished patients, should avoid it. Recent guidance for moderate to advanced non-dialysis CKD supports a low-protein approach in metabolically stable patients, and also encourages eating more plant-based foods than animal- based foods, with careful monitoring in advanced CKD. Working with a clinician or kidney dietitian is therefore important, because dietary needs often change as CKD progresses.

chunks.section: Recommended overall dietary patterns and preferred foods
chunks.text: For many people with CKD, the best overall pattern is a mostly plant-forward, minimally processed diet rather than a diet centered on red meat, processed foods, and salt. Good choices usually include vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, fish, and unsaturated fats, with adjustments if potassium or phosphorus become a problem. In general, the dietary patterns most often favored for CKD are healthy, whole-food patterns such as the Mediterranean diet, DASH-style eating, and plant-dominant diets. These patterns emphasize fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, and fiber, while keeping sodium low and limiting saturated fat, refined sugar, and processed meats; they have also been linked with better cardiovascular outcomes and slower kidney decline or lower CKD risk in many studies. A practical way to eat is to build meals mostly from minimally processed foods and home-cooked dishes: vegetables, fruits, rice or other grains, beans or other legumes when allowed, and modest portions of lean protein. When available and tolerated, whole grains, high-fiber carbohydrates, and mixed fruits and vegetables are preferred over refined starches and sugary foods, and fats should come mainly from unsaturated sources such as olive, canola, or flaxseed oils rather than butter or other saturated fats. (Kalantar- Zadeh et al., 2017) Many recent reviews and guidelines also favor shifting more of the diet toward plant foods than animal foods, especially replacing red and processed meat with vegetables, grains, legumes, and other plant foods. This can lower dietary acid load and may put less stress on the kidneys; fruit and vegetable intake may also help counter metabolic acidosis, which can worsen with

Preferred protein-containing foods within this overall pattern are usually fish, poultry, and plant protein sources, with attention to the patient's full nutrition prescription. Fish is often encouraged in place of red and processed meat, and several sources describe plant-dominant low-protein patterns that use at least half of protein from plant sources and rely on unprocessed foods. So, foods that are often good staples for CKD patients include fresh or low-sodium vegetables and fruits, whole grains or other high-fiber starches, beans and legumes if they fit potassium and phosphorus goals, fish, small amounts of lean meats or poultry, and unsaturated fats. If fresh produce is hard to get, low-sodium and low-sugar canned fruits and vegetables can also be used. This means eating sausages, cold cuts, fast food, packaged snacks, sugar-sweetened drinks, cakes, cookies, and similar foods only rarely, if at all, because these foods tend to worsen diet quality and can add sodium, highly absorbable phosphorus additives, and excess sugar. chunks.section: Protein intake and protein sources
chunks.text: In non-dialysis CKD, protein often needs to be moderated rather than increased. Many guidelines support about 0.8 g/kg/ day for metabolically stable adults with stages 3 to 5 CKD, avoiding high-protein diets and often favoring more plant protein over red and processed meat. Protein is one of the most important parts of a CKD diet because both too much and too little can cause problems. In metabolically stable adults with CKD stages 3 to 5 who are not on dialysis, guidelines support protein restriction, commonly around 0.8 g/kg/day, to help delay kidney failure and improve symptoms or quality of life. Some reviews describe low-protein diets in the range of about 0.6 to 0.8 g/kg/day, and very low-protein diets around 0.3 to 0.4 g/kg/day are sometimes used in selected predialysis patients, usually with ketoacid or essential amino acid support and close supervision. (Rodelo- Haad et al., 2025) Just as important, CKD patients generally should avoid high-protein eating patterns, especially diets that replace carbohydrates with large amounts of meat or other protein foods. High protein intake, particularly above about 1.3 g/kg/day in adults at risk of CKD progression, has been linked to intraglomerular hypertension, hyperfiltration, proteinuria, and faster kidney damage, so high-protein weight-loss diets are usually a poor fit for CKD. When choosing protein foods, many sources favor shifting away from animal-heavy patterns and toward more plant-based protein. Plant-dominant low-protein approaches, often with at least half of protein coming from plant sources, may help by lowering acid load, reducing gut-derived uremic toxins, improving phosphorus control, and causing less glomerular hyperfiltration than animal

chunks.source: Kidney Disease Diet Recommendations, Food Choices, and Foods to Avoid.pdf
chunks.section: Protein intake and protein sources
chunks.text: patterns and toward more plant-based protein. Plant-dominant low-protein approaches, often with at least half of protein coming from plant sources, may help by lowering acid load, reducing gut-derived uremic toxins, improving phosphorus control, and causing less glomerular hyperfiltration than animal protein. In practical terms, this usually means using more beans, lentils, soy foods, and other plant proteins when allowed, and choosing fish or poultry more often than red or processed meat. That said, protein restriction is not right for every patient. If someone is undernourished, losing weight unintentionally, has protein-energy wasting, or has other signs that nutrition is poor, preserving protein intake may be more important than restricting it. Older adults need especially careful balancing, and some patients should avoid or postpone protein restriction until nutritional status is stable. (Piccoli et al., 2023) So, for most non-dialysis CKD patients, the practical message is: do not follow a high-protein diet; aim for a clinician-guided moderate or low protein target; get more protein from plant foods, fish, and poultry; and keep red and processed meats smaller and less frequent. Because protein targets change with CKD stage, dialysis status, and nutrition risk, the exact amount should be set with a kidney dietitian or clinician rather than guessed.

chunks.section: Foods and nutrients to limit or avoid
chunks.text: The main things CKD patients often need to limit are salt, processed foods, excess protein, and sometimes foods high in phosphorus or potassium. The exact "avoid" list depends on blood tests and CKD stage, so some foods are restricted only when phosphorus or potassium are high. Salt and high-sodium foods are one of the biggest things to cut back on. A low-salt diet is a cornerstone of CKD care, with many sources recommending sodium intake below about 2 to 2.3 g per day. In practice, this means limiting added salt and avoiding foods like pickles, papad, chutneys, sauces, salted butter, salted nuts, canned foods, ready-to-eat meals, fast food, and foods made with monosodium glutamate. (Sinha et al., 2024) Ultra-processed and packaged foods should be kept low. These foods are often major sources of sodium and may also contain phosphate additives, which are especially important to avoid in CKD. Processed foods are repeatedly listed among the foods to limit for both salt and phosphorus control. Do not follow a high-protein diet. Although protein needs were discussed above, it is worth stating plainly in an "avoid" list: CKD patients generally should avoid high-protein eating patterns, especially in stages 1 to 2 if intake is above about 1.3 g/kg/day, and often need lower protein intake in stages 3 to 5 before dialysis. Foods high in phosphorus may need to be limited, especially when phosphorus is high or CKD is more advanced. Nuts, seeds, beans, and some dairy foods are "healthy" foods in general, but they are not always free foods in CKD. They can provide useful nutrients and protein, yet many are high in phosphorus and sometimes potassium, so portions may need to be limited rather than eaten freely. Hard cheeses are a concern for both salt and phosphorus, and even fresh dairy may need restriction in some patients. Routine potassium restriction is not suggested unless serum potassium is high and other causes of hyperkalemia have been addressed. chunks.section: Potassium, phosphorus, and fluid restrictions: when they apply
chunks.text: Potassium, phosphorus, and fluid limits are not automatic for every person with CKD. They are used when kidney function is more reduced, when blood tests are abnormal, or when symptoms like swelling and poor urine output make them necessary. Potassium restriction should be targeted, not routine. In mild to moderate CKD, some experts argue that patients may actually benefit from more fiber, fruits, vegetables, and potassium-rich plant foods, rather than avoiding them too early, because these foods can support overall diet quality and kidney health (Kaesler et al., 2021). A plant-forward or modified DASH-style pattern can therefore still fit many patients with earlier CKD, but this changes once potassium excretion becomes impaired. In advanced CKD, or in people with a history of hyperkalemia, fruits and vegetables are often limited because of the risk of high potassium, and even DASH-type eating patterns or potassium-enriched salt substitutes can be harmful. The practical point is that foods rich in bioavailable potassium should be adjusted with dietitian guidance, especially in CKD G3 to G5 patients who have had hyperkalemia. Phosphorus restriction also depends on CKD severity and lab results, rather than applying equally to everyone. As kidney function declines, phosphorus is harder to clear, so patients with more advanced CKD or high serum phosphorus often need closer control of high-phosphorus foods and phosphate additives (Model- Generated). chunks.section: Diet quality, food preparation, and counseling considerations
chunks.text: A kidney-friendly diet is not just about which foods to avoid. It also depends on food quality, how meals are prepared, portion size, label reading, and regular follow-up with a kidney dietitian or clinician. Food quality matters because two diets can contain similar nutrients on paper but affect kidney health very differently in real life. In general, patients do best when they choose mostly fresh or minimally processed foods, cook at home more often, and keep portions steady rather than eating large restaurant or takeaway meals. Simple cooking methods such as boiling, steaming, baking, grilling, and pressure- cooking are usually better than deep-frying or relying on packaged sauces, seasoning mixes, or instant foods, which often add a lot of sodium and phosphate additives. For patients who need potassium control, cooking methods can also help; for example, cutting and boiling some vegetables in extra water can lower potassium content, though this should be used only when potassium restriction is actually needed. Reading food labels is also a key skill. Patients are often advised to check sodium per serving, watch serving size, and look for ingredients that suggest phosphate additives, such as words containing "phos" (Model- Generated). "Low-fat," "multigrain," "high-protein," or "healthy" packaged foods are not always kidney-friendly, because they may still contain a lot of salt, potassium additives, phosphorus additives, or protein (Model- Generated). Salt substitutes also need caution, since many are made with potassium chloride and can be unsafe in patients at risk for hyperkalemia. chunks.section: Background
chunks.text: There is no single "stomach-problem diet" that works for everyone. Broad elimination plans are common, but the best diet depends on the cause of symptoms and should be tailored when possible. People with stomach or gut symptoms are often given broad, one-size-fits-all diet plans, such as exclusion diets, low-FODMAP diets, gluten-free diets, lactose-free diets, NICE-style advice, or wheat-free diets, but the evidence does not support the idea that one approach is right for all patients. Instead, diet should be guided by the likely cause of symptoms: if H. pylori is present, eradication treatment is needed, and if food intolerance or malabsorption is found, a personalized diet plan with a registered dietitian is recommended. This means the best advice is usually to match the diet to the diagnosis rather than assume every patient should avoid the same foods.

chunks.section: Core eating pattern and meal habits
chunks.text: A good starting pattern for many stomach or gut problems is to eat small, regular meals, eat slowly, and avoid very large or rushed meals. Also, drink enough fluid, mainly water or herbal tea, and keep a simple food diary to spot personal triggers. Use a regular meal pattern. Try to eat at set times instead of skipping meals or eating erratically. Several sources suggest 3 main meals, with 2–3 snacks or small meals through the day, depending on what feels best. Choose smaller meals more often. Small, frequent meals can reduce stomach stretching and may be easier to digest than a few large meals. Avoid both overeating and, when possible, long gaps that lead to very large meals later. Eat slowly and in a calm setting. Take time to chew well and avoid hurried eating. Guidance for IBS and other stomach complaints repeatedly stresses that how you eat can matter as much as the food itself. Drink enough fluid every day. A common target is about 1.5–2 liters a day or about 8 cups, mainly water and often herbal tea. This is especially important if diarrhea is present or if fiber is being increased for constipation. Prefer easy-to-digest foods when symptoms are active. During flares or sudden symptoms, many papers suggest light, soft, digestible foods, and avoiding foods that are very rough, very hot, very cold, or strongly irritating. Keep a food and symptom diary. This can help you find your own trigger foods instead of cutting out many foods at once. Self-monitoring is commonly advised before trying stricter

chunks.section: Condition-specific dietary strategies
chunks.text: The best diet depends on the condition causing the stomach or gut symptoms. For IBS, a low-FODMAP diet has the strongest support; for IBD, diet is often adjusted to symptom phase; and for a few specific disorders, targeted sugar or allergen elimination may be used. For irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), a low-FODMAP diet is the main targeted diet to consider. It is the most consistently supported diet for improving overall IBS symptoms, and several guidelines recommend a limited trial rather than permanent strict avoidance. The usual approach is short-term restriction, then gradual reintroduction to find which FODMAP groups actually trigger symptoms. This works best with dietitian support because the diet is restrictive and can lead to unnecessary food avoidance if done alone. In IBS, start by targeting common symptom triggers before wider restriction. Advice often includes reducing gas-producing foods, and in some patients trying lactose avoidance if milk seems to trigger symptoms. Lower intake of fat, insoluble fiber, caffeine, bloating foods, spicy foods, alcohol, carbonated drinks, and sometimes limiting fruit to about 3 portions a day may also help. Do not assume gluten is the problem in IBS unless celiac disease is present. A gluten-free diet is sometimes used, but it is not routinely recommended without celiac disease, because many wheat foods also contain fructans, which are FODMAPs and may be the real trigger. (Vasant et al., 2021) Some IBS patients may benefit from individualized fiber or starch-sugar changes. For short bowel or malabsorption states, diet needs a different structure. Suggested measures can include avoiding hyperosmolar drinks, controlling simple sugars, using some starch-containing foods, limiting lactose, choosing the type of fiber based on symptoms, lowering fat, and avoiding oxalate in some cases. This is a specialist area and usually needs individualized medical nutrition advice. If a formal exclusion diet is used, it should be temporary and structured. Older IBS studies found benefit from supervised elimination diets, but the key step was always to reintroduce foods one at a time and identify the true trigger foods, instead of staying on a very restricted diet long term.

chunks.section: Recommended foods and foods to prefer
chunks.text: In many stomach or gut problems, the safest foods to prefer are simple, soft, lower-fat, and easy to digest. Commonly favored choices include lean proteins, rice or oats, cooked vegetables, bananas, yogurt or lactose-free dairy if tolerated, and fluids such as water or clear soups. Choose lean, lower-fat protein foods. Good options often include lean meat, fish, poultry, eggs, and in some cases beans if they are tolerated. For chronic gastritis, moderate amounts of lean beef or lean lamb may be used, while fattier cuts are less suitable. Use simple starches and grains that are easy on the stomach. Common examples include rice, potatoes, noodles, oats, crackers, toast, and in low-FODMAP plans, gluten-free grains such as rice. These are especially often used when diarrhea or active symptoms are present. Prefer soft, bland, well-cooked foods during flares. When symptoms are active, foods such as mashed potatoes, cooked carrots, boiled chicken, stewed fruit, cooked oats, pureed soups, pureed vegetables, smoothies, and ground lean meats are commonly recommended because they are easier to tolerate. Choose fruits and vegetables in forms you tolerate well. Papers commonly mention bananas as a well- tolerated fruit, and recommend using a variety of fruits and vegetables with the texture adjusted to symptoms, such as cooked, stewed, blended, or pureed forms when needed. If using a low-FODMAP approach, favor the foods allowed within that plan. Examples given include meat, poultry, fish, eggs, lactose-free dairy, rice, bananas, spinach, most nuts, and most herbs and spices. If dairy is wanted, use the type that matches tolerance. If dairy is wanted, use the type that matches tolerance. Some patients do better with lactose-free dairy, while others may tolerate plain yogurt better than milk. Fermented dairy is also used in some IBD-focused diets. Fermented and probiotic foods may help some patients, especially in IBD-style plans. Examples mentioned include plain yogurt, fermented vegetables, and kimchi. Include soluble-fiber and prebiotic foods if they are tolerated. Examples listed in IBD-AID-type guidance include oats, bananas, ground flaxseeds, chia seeds, garlic, onions, and asparagus, though tolerance can vary and some of these are not suitable in a low-FODMAP phase. Use healthy fats in modest amounts rather than heavy, greasy foods. Some plans favor nuts and olive oil and suggest keeping saturated fat low. During short episodes of diarrhea or stomach upset, start simply. A short period of clear liquids with electrolyte replacement, then foods like bananas, rice, applesauce, toast, soup, oats, potatoes, and crackers, is a common practical approach. Fresh, minimally processed foods are generally preferred. Some recent guidance suggests increasing fresh fruits, vegetables, and fermented foods like yogurt, while reducing reliance on heavily processed foods.

chunks.section: Foods and beverages commonly avoided or limited
chunks.text: Foods most often limited are those that clearly trigger symptoms, especially high-FODMAP foods, insoluble fiber, very fatty meals, alcohol, coffee, spicy foods, and fizzy drinks. Dairy is not always a problem, but milk or other dairy may need to be limited if lactose intolerance is present. High-FODMAP foods are one of the most common groups to limit, especially in IBS. These include foods rich in poorly absorbed sugars such as wheat, onions, garlic, pulses/legumes, milk, honey, apples, pears, and some sweeteners like sorbitol. These foods can worsen bloating, pain, gas, and diarrhea in some patients. Foods high in insoluble fiber may need to be reduced if they worsen symptoms. Several IBS-focused papers specifically mention insoluble fiber as a symptom trigger and advise shifting away from foods with higher amounts of it when symptoms are active. Gas-producing foods are often limited when bloating is a major problem. Common examples listed across papers include beans or legumes, onions, cauliflower, celery, broccoli, wheat bran, carrots, raisins, bananas, apricots, prunes or plums. Not all of these cause trouble for every person, but they are common foods to test as possible triggers. Very fatty, greasy, and highly processed foods are often cut back. Guidance commonly suggests limiting high-fat foods, and some newer diet strategies also avoid processed meats treated with sugar or starch such as bacon, pies, and sausage, as well as heavily processed breakfast cereals. Alcohol, coffee, and carbonated drinks are commonly limited. These are repeatedly listed as drinks that can worsen gut symptoms, especially bloating, pain, reflux-like discomfort, or diarrhea in sensitive patients.

chunks.text: bacon, pies, and sausage, as well as heavily processed breakfast cereals. Alcohol, coffee, and carbonated drinks are commonly limited. These are repeatedly listed as drinks that can worsen gut symptoms, especially bloating, pain, reflux-like discomfort, or diarrhea in sensitive patients. Spicy foods are commonly avoided if they trigger symptoms. They are among the foods most often reported as troublesome in functional bowel symptoms and are frequently restricted in practical diet advice. Dairy may need to be limited, but only in the right patients. If a person has lactase deficiency or lactose intolerance, dairy can worsen symptoms and may need to be avoided; however, this does not mean all patients with stomach problems should cut out dairy, since some can tolerate lactose-free dairy well. Some condiments and pickled foods may also irritate symptoms in some people. Older practical guidance for IBS specifically lists vinegar, mustard, ketchup, and pickled foods as items some patients may want to avoid. In starch- and sucrose-reduction approaches, sugary foods are limited. These plans ask patients to avoid sucrose-containing foods and reduce starch-heavy refined foods, while using less processed grain choices instead. The most useful rule is to limit foods that repeatedly trigger your own symptoms, not to avoid every "bad" food forever. Studies note that patients often avoid many foods, sometimes even during remission, so it is better to use a structured, personal approach rather than broad long-term restriction without a clear reason.

chunks.section: Personalization, reintroduction, and supervision
chunks.text: The best diet plan is the one that matches the cause of symptoms and the foods each person actually reacts to. If foods are removed, they should usually be added back in a planned way, and restrictive diets are safest with medical or dietitian support. Diet for stomach or gut problems should be personal, not based on a long list of foods to avoid forever. A good next step after basic meal changes is to look for patterns, test likely triggers one at a time, and match the diet to the diagnosis. If a short-term elimination diet is used, the goal is usually not permanent restriction but a careful reintroduction phase to see which foods truly cause symptoms and which can stay in the diet. This helps reduce unnecessary food avoidance and lowers the risk of poor nutrition. Medical review is important if there are alarm features such as weight loss, bleeding, anemia, trouble swallowing, persistent vomiting, fever, dehydration, or symptoms that do not improve. A registered dietitian can help most when the diet is complex, symptoms are ongoing, or whole food groups are being removed, such as with low-FODMAP, allergy elimination, malabsorption, or IBD-related plans.
